title: The shadow behind the core
teaches: How missing waves on the far side of the Earth revealed the core, and how S waves showed it is liquid

parts.title: Late waves from the far side

blocks.text: Lesson D1 ended with a dense core proposed from the Earth's weight. Seismographs offered a way to look for it directly. In 1906 Richard Dixon Oldham, a geologist with the Geological Survey of India who had studied the great Assam earthquake of 1897, gathered records of distant earthquakes and plotted how long their waves took to arrive at different distances. Waves to nearby and middling distances fitted a steady pattern. Waves that had to cross the middle of the Earth, to stations nearly on the opposite side, arrived noticeably later than the pattern predicted, as if something in the centre slowed them.

Oldham's data were sparse, and he was not sure which kind of wave he was seeing. But his conclusion was right: the Earth has a central core in which earthquake waves travel more slowly than in the rock around it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Oldham (1906) found that waves crossing the centre of the Earth arrived late.
He proposed a central core where waves travel more slowly.

blocks.text: To see what a slow core does, follow a wave through the Earth. Distances around the Earth are given as angles measured from the Earth's centre: a station 90° from a quake is a quarter of the way around, 180° is directly opposite. In the mantle, rock gets stiffer with depth, so waves travel faster the deeper they go. A wave heading down at a slant is therefore bent gradually back toward the surface, the same way light bends in a mirage, and it comes up again some distance away. The steeper it starts, the deeper it goes and the farther away it emerges.

Now add a core where waves travel more slowly. A wave crossing into slower material bends toward the steeper direction, like light entering water from air. Waves that only just miss the core travel on through the mantle and come up as far as about 100° away. Waves that only just hit it are bent sharply inward, cross the core, and are bent again as they leave, emerging much farther around the Earth, beyond about 140°. Between those distances, no direct P wave arrives at all: there is a **shadow zone**.

blocks.caption: Wave paths from an earthquake at the top, through half of the Earth, drawn to scale. Every sixth path of many is drawn. The speeds in the mantle follow measured values, simplified; you set the core.
blocks.task: Add a core that casts a P-wave shadow starting near 104°

blocks.text: In 1914 Beno Gutenberg, then at Göttingen in Germany and later at Caltech, used many more records to map the shadow: direct P waves disappear beyond about 104° from a quake and reappear at about 140°. From the edges of the shadow he calculated the depth of the core's surface: 2,900 kilometres, a little under halfway to the centre. The modern figure is 2,890. The core's radius is 3,480 kilometres, just over half the Earth's, which also fits the density and the moment of inertia of lesson D1.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Waves speed up with depth in the mantle and curve back to the surface.
Waves entering the slower core are bent inward, leaving a shadow zone where no direct P waves arrive, from about 104° to 140°.
Gutenberg (1914) put the top of the core at 2,900 km depth; the modern value is 2,890 km.

blocks.text: S waves told a more extreme story. They do arrive at stations up to about 104°, but beyond that no direct S waves arrive at all, anywhere on the far side of the Earth. Lesson D2 explained why that would be: S waves cannot travel through liquid.

In 1926 the British geophysicist Harold Jeffreys made the case in a different way. The Moon's and Sun's gravity raise tides in the solid Earth as well as in the oceans: the ground itself rises and falls by about 30 centimetres twice a day. How much it does so depends on how stiff the Earth is overall. The mantle's stiffness was known from its S-wave speeds, and Jeffreys showed that if the core were as stiff as the mantle, the Earth would flex less than it does. The core had to be far less rigid, and the simplest answer was that it is liquid. Molten iron, kept liquid by the heat inside the Earth, fits the density, the shadow and the tides.
Use the switch in the figure to send S waves instead of P. Every S wave that reaches the core stops there, and the S shadow covers the whole far side of the Earth.

blocks.caption: The Earth's layers to scale, with the depths of their boundaries.

blocks.text: A liquid iron core also explains something the course met in lesson 9. The Earth's magnetic field, which reverses from time to time and leaves the stripes on the sea floor, is generated by the slow churning of the molten iron, which conducts electricity, as the planet loses heat. A field that flips its direction could not come from a solid magnet; it needs a moving, conducting fluid.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: No direct S waves arrive beyond about 104°, because they cannot cross the core.
Jeffreys (1926) showed from the Earth's tides that the core cannot be rigid: it is liquid.
Churning molten iron in the outer core generates the Earth's magnetic field.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the core
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why do waves heading down into the mantle curve back up to the surface?
choices: Waves travel faster with depth in the mantle, which bends them back upward
They bounce off the bottom of the crust
The Earth's gravity pulls them back up
items.why: A wave travelling into faster material bends away from the steeper direction, so a wave going down at a slant gradually turns back toward the surface.

items.ask: What causes the P-wave shadow zone?
choices: Waves entering the slower core are bent sharply inward, so none arrive directly between about 104° and 140°
The core absorbs all P waves
The shadow zone is where the oceans are
items.why: Waves just missing the core emerge before about 104°; those just hitting it are bent inward and emerge beyond about 140°. Nothing direct lands in between.

items.ask: Why does no direct S wave reach the far side of the Earth?
choices: The outer core is liquid, and S waves cannot pass through liquid
S waves are too slow to cross the Earth before fading
S waves are reflected by the Moho
items.why: S waves need a material that springs back when sheared. Liquid iron does not, so S waves stop at the core.

items.ask: How did Jeffreys use the tides to show the core is liquid?
choices: The solid Earth flexes more under tides than it would if the core were as stiff as the mantle
Ocean tides are higher above the core
The tides make the core spin faster
items.why: The Earth's overall stiffness, measured from its tidal flexing, was too low for a rigid core.

items.ask: How far down is the top of the core?
items.why: Gutenberg calculated 2,900 km from the edges of the shadow zone in 1914. The modern value is 2,890 km.

learned: Oldham (1906) found waves crossing the Earth's centre arrived late; Gutenberg (1914) mapped the P shadow zone and put the core's top at 2,900 km.
Waves bend inward entering the slower core, which leaves a shadow from about 104° to 140°.
S waves stop at the core, and Jeffreys (1926) showed from tides that it is liquid; its churning makes the magnetic field.
